transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because things have just gotten to a point where I can't really manage the noise in my own mind anymore. It’s hard to even know where to begin, honestly, but... I just can't shake this feeling that I've completely failed. I look back at my life, at my family, and it just hits me so hard that I failed as a father. And not just that, but as a useful person in general. 

I spent all those years in grad school, you know, I thought I had a path, I thought I was going to be someone who contributed, but now I’m not doing anything for anyone. And the worst part is that it never stops. The guilt, I mean. It just keeps looping in my head, over and over, playing every mistake and every shortcoming on repeat from the moment I wake up. It’s like I can't even hold a normal conversation or sit in a quiet room because the thoughts are so loud. It just loops and loops until it completely wears me down, and I... I get to this place where I honestly feel like I don't deserve much of a future. 

I mean, what kind of future are you supposed to have when you've let everyone down and you have nothing of value left to offer? Why should things get better for someone who caused so much disappointment? It just feels incredibly heavy, and it takes up all the space in my brain, and I just... I don't know how to turn it off. So I guess that's what brings me in.
Have you felt this way — down, hopeless, or critical of yourself — most of the day, nearly every day, for at least the past two years?

Two years? Oh, no. No, not two years. I mean, I've always had my regrets, sure, but this... this intense, suffocating feeling where I can't even function and the thoughts are just screaming at me? That really just started about a month ago. 

It was right around the time my daughter left for college. She decided to go out of state, you see, which is great for her, really, it's a good school, but... well, ever since we dropped her off, it’s like a switch flipped in my brain. We spent weeks packing, buying things for her dorm, and I kept busy, but then we got back to the house and it was just... empty. I walked past her room and the door was open and it just hit me all at once. Every mistake I ever made raising her, every time I fell short, every way I failed to provide the kind of life she deserved because I'm not working and putting my degree to use... it all just came crashing down on me. 

And it hasn't stopped since. For the past month, every single day, from the minute I wake up and realize she's not down the hall, the guilt just starts playing on a loop. So, no, it hasn't been years of this specific nightmare, just about four weeks since she moved away. But honestly, doctor, it feels like it’s been a lifetime already because there's just no break from it. I just sit there looking at her old bedroom door and thinking about how I can never get those years back to do it right...
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things the way you used to — activities or hobbies that you used to find pleasurable or meaningful?

Well, yes. Yes, I suppose that's true. I mean, it's not like I was out climbing mountains or, you know, going to fancy galas before, but I had things that mattered to me. Things I used to actually look forward to. 

Like my model railway... I don't know if I mentioned that, but I have this whole setup down in the basement. HO scale, mostly mid-century locomotives, and I was in the middle of building this incredibly detailed switching yard. I'd spend hours down there, getting the ballast just right, painting the little figures... it was meticulous work, but it was soothing, you know? It gave me a sense of accomplishment. But now? Now the trains just sit there, half-built on the table. The glue is probably dried out in the bottles. I walk down the stairs sometimes, just to look at it, and I just feel... nothing. Or worse than nothing, I feel like it's a monument to how useless I am. I can't even bring myself to pick up a paintbrush. It just seems so utterly pointless. 

And it's not just the trains, either. It's the Cubs games. My daughter and I, we used to watch the Cubs all the time. It was our thing. Even when she got older and busier with high school, she'd still come sit on the couch with me for at least a few innings. We'd talk about the roster, complain about the bullpen... it was just nice. It was a connection. But now that she's gone, I tried turning a game on the other night. I thought, you know, maybe it'll feel normal. Maybe it'll be a distraction. But I couldn't even make it through the first inning. The sound of the crowd, the announcers... it just felt hollow. It just reminded me that she wasn't there, and that I'm just this guy sitting alone in a quiet house, not contributing anything to the world. So I turned the TV off. I haven't turned it back on since. Even the thought of opening a game on the TV just feels completely pointless now. Everything just feels... flat. Like all the color has been drained out of my life, and I'm just going through the motions, but even the motions are too heavy to keep up with.
Have you been feeling fatigued or lacking energy most days, even when you haven’t done anything physically or mentally demanding?

Fatigue? Oh, absolutely. It’s... it's honestly overwhelming. I mean, it’s not like I’m running marathons or, you know, even going into an office anymore, so you'd think I’d be well-rested, right? I spend most of my time just sitting around the house. But it’s this deep, heavy exhaustion that just never goes away. 

It’s like... well, the other day, I needed to bring a basket of laundry upstairs. Just a regular load, nothing crazy. And I stood at the bottom of the stairs looking up at them, and it felt like I was staring at Mount Everest. I finally picked up the basket, and every step... it honestly felt like I was moving through wet cement. My arms felt heavy, my legs felt like lead. I had to stop halfway up just to catch my breath, and not because my heart was racing or anything, but just because my body simply didn't want to move anymore. 

And it’s not just physical stuff, either. Even something as simple as sorting the mail... I went out to the mailbox, which is just at the end of the driveway, mind you, and brought in a handful of envelopes. I sat down at the kitchen table to go through them—junk mail, a couple of bills, you know the drill—and I just stared at them. The sheer effort of opening an envelope, of looking at a piece of paper and figuring out what to do with it... it was just too much. I ended up leaving it all in a pile on the table and going back to the couch. 

It doesn't matter how long I've been in bed, either. I could lie there for ten hours, twelve hours, and I wake up feeling just as drained as when I went to sleep. It’s this constant, pervasive lack of energy that just drags me down all day long, no matter what I do or don't do. I just... I don't have the energy for anything anymore. Not for the trains, not for the mail, not even to walk up a flight of stairs without feeling like I've run a decathlon. It's just exhausting, doctor. Completely exhausting.
Have you been having trouble sleeping — either not being able to fall asleep, waking up during the night, or sleeping much more than usual?

Sleep? Oh... sleep is just a joke at this point. It's honestly a whole other battle. You'd think, given how completely exhausted I am all day, like I was just saying, that I'd just pass out the second my head hits the pillow. But no. No, it doesn't work like that at all. 

The nights might actually be the worst part of all of this, if you can believe it. Because when evening comes and I finally go up to bed... the house is just so quiet. It's too quiet. When my daughter was here, there was always some background noise, you know? The faint sound of her music, or her talking on the phone, or just the floorboards creaking. But now... it’s just this heavy, dead silence. I just lie there in the dark for hours. I stare at the ceiling, I flip the pillow, I look at the clock... and I just lie there, wide awake, listening to the silence. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off—usually just from pure, physical exhaustion—it never lasts. It’s like clockwork. I’ll jolt awake, and I’ll look over at the red numbers on the alarm clock, and it's always right around three or four in the morning. The absolute dead of night. And once my eyes are open at 3 AM, that's it. I'm done. There is absolutely no chance I'm getting back to sleep. 

I try, I really do try to close my eyes and force it, but my mind just... it just turns on and starts running at a hundred miles an hour. And it's never good thoughts. It immediately starts running through everything I've ever messed up. It’s like a highlight reel of all my failures. I lie there thinking about how I have this graduate degree that I'm doing absolutely nothing with, how I haven't provided the life my family deserved, every little time I lost my temper or wasn't there enough for my daughter... just a relentless loop of every mistake, every regret. You can't sleep when your own brain is just screaming at you about what a massive disappointment you are. So I just end up lying there, trapped in my own head, until the sun finally comes up. And by then, I'm already too exhausted to face the day.
Have you ever experienced a period in your life before this recent one where you felt this level of hopelessness, guilt, or loss of interest in things you used to enjoy?

No... no, honestly, I haven't. I mean, sure, I've had bad days, or even bad weeks. Who hasn't, right? Life gets stressful. I remember back when I was finishing up my graduate degree, the pressure was just immense. I'd have these moments where I felt completely overwhelmed, maybe a little down, wondering if I was ever going to get through my thesis and all the expectations. Or, you know, when my daughter was little and money was tight, there were nights I'd sit up worrying about how we'd pay for everything, feeling the weight of being a provider. 

But even then... even when things were really hard, it was never... it was never *this*. With those things, there was always a light at the end of the tunnel. I always knew, deep down, that if I just kept pushing, things would get better. I could still laugh at a joke, or I could still go down to the basement and tinker with the trains and actually feel some relief. I could still enjoy a baseball game and forget my troubles for a few hours. 

But this? This is entirely different. I've never experienced anything close to this level of just... absolute, crushing emptiness. It’s like a completely different species of feeling. I used to think I was a pretty resilient guy, you know? I thought I could handle whatever life threw at me, that I had a good head on my shoulders. I look back at those times I thought I was struggling before, and they honestly seem like a walk in the park compared to this. I just never knew a person's mind could turn on them so completely, where you just feel utterly hopeless and guilty for even taking up space in the world. So, no, doctor, this is all completely new to me. And it's terrifying, frankly, because I don't know how to get back to the guy who could just shake off a bad week.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently — like eating much less or much more than usual, or losing or gaining a significant amount of weight?

Appetite? Yeah... yeah, that's gone too. It's funny you ask that because I was just thinking about it the other day when I was trying to put on a pair of pants I haven't worn in a while. I had to pull my belt tight, like, two notches tighter than usual. I hadn't really noticed until then, but I guess I've lost quite a bit of weight. It’s not like I’m trying to, believe me. I just... I don't care about food anymore. 

It used to be that dinner was a whole thing, you know? My wife would cook, or I'd grill something out back, and we'd sit down together. It was an event. But now? Most days, I just don't even bother making a real meal. The thought of getting up, figuring out what to cook, getting the ingredients out, standing by the stove... it just goes back to that exhaustion I was talking about earlier. It's just too much effort. It feels completely pointless to go through all that trouble just for myself. 

So, what happens is, I just sit there on the couch, or I'm lying in bed, and I honestly just forget to eat. The whole day will go by, and I won't even realize I haven't had anything until it's, like, eight or nine at night and my stomach starts making these awful hollow noises. And even then, when I finally realize I should probably put something in my stomach, I don't have the energy or the desire to actually make anything substantial. I'll just shuffle into the kitchen and pop a couple of pieces of bread in the toaster. Or I'll pour a bowl of cereal. That's about all I can manage. Just dry toast or a bowl of Cheerios, standing there in the dark kitchen. And even then, I'm just forcing it down. It all tastes like cardboard anyway. There's no joy in it, no flavor, no satisfaction. It's just... fuel, I guess, but barely even that. So yeah, I'm definitely eating a lot less, and the weight is just falling off because of it.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or feeling restless and unable to sit still?

Restless? No... no, definitely not restless. I mean, to be restless, you have to actually have some kind of energy, right? Like a nervous energy or a need to do something. And I have absolutely zero energy. It's funny you ask about sitting still, because sitting still is pretty much the only thing I actually *do* anymore. 

I have this old leather recliner in the living room—it’s right by the front window where you can see out onto the street—and I’ll just sit there. For hours and hours. I don't fidget, I don't pace the floors, I don't tap my foot... I just sit. It’s almost like I’m glued to the chair. I'll watch the cars go by, or the mailman doing his route, and I just feel completely rooted there, like I'm just another heavy piece of furniture in the room. So no, I'm definitely not unable to sit still. If anything, I'm way too still. I just want to sink into the cushions and disappear. 

And as for moving or speaking slowly... I really don't think so? I mean, I'm not exactly sprinting around the house, obviously, because of how completely exhausted I am, but when I do finally get up to, say, go make that piece of toast I mentioned earlier, I just walk normally, I think. I don't feel like I'm moving through molasses or slow motion or anything like that. 

And my speech... well, you're listening to me right now. I feel like I'm talking at the exact same pace I always have. My wife hasn't pointed anything out about it, either. We don't talk nearly as much these days, mostly because I just don't have the drive to hold a real conversation, but when I do say something, it comes out normal. I haven't noticed my words dragging. I'm just... I'm just completely drained, you know? But not physically slow or restless. Just stuck.
Have you had any thoughts about ending your life or not wanting to live anymore?

I... well, I wouldn't say I have a specific plan or anything like that. I'm not sitting here actively figuring out how to do it. But... wanting to live? That's a much harder question to answer lately. Because, honestly, there are so many nights now where I just lie there in the dark, and I think about how much easier it would be if I just didn't wake up the next morning. You know? If I just drifted off and that was it. No more waking up to this heavy, crushing emptiness I was telling you about. No more dragging myself out of bed just to sit in that recliner all day feeling like a burden. Just... peace. Just quiet. I've had that thought a lot, actually. Just hoping I'd go to sleep and the universe would just sort of take care of it for me, so I wouldn't have to face another single day feeling like this. 

But then... there was this thing that happened a few days ago that really, really shook me up. It actually scared me quite a bit. I was sitting at the dining room table—which I rarely do anymore, like I said, I'm usually just glued to that chair by the window—but I had my laptop open, and I had all these folders pulled out. The bank statements, the life insurance policy, the mortgage documents. And I was organizing them. I was making sure all the account numbers were clearly listed out on this yellow legal pad, writing down the passwords, checking the beneficiaries to make sure everything was completely up to date. I was just meticulously going through every single financial detail we have. 

And I was sitting there, writing it all out, and it suddenly hit me like a ton of bricks *why* I was doing it. I wasn't just doing our regular monthly budget or checking our balances. I was... I was getting things ready. I was setting it all up so that if I wasn't here, my wife wouldn't have to struggle to figure out where everything was. I was preparing it all for someone else to take over. And when I realized that—when I caught myself actually preparing for not being around—it terrified me. It really did. Because I didn't even consciously sit down with the intention to do that, my brain just sort of took me there on autopilot. So, I guess... I guess the thoughts are definitely there, even if I'm trying to ignore them. It's just getting so incredibly hard to keep carrying all this weight every day.

Have you ever experienced a period of time where you felt unusually high, overly energetic, or extremely confident — maybe even to the point where others noticed you were acting out of character or needed less sleep?

Unusually high? Energetic? No... no, I can honestly say I have never felt anything even close to that. It’s actually almost hard to even imagine feeling that way right now, to be perfectly honest with you. I mean, you’re asking about having too much energy, and like I was saying earlier about the toast and just sitting in that recliner all day, I barely have the energy to just exist right now. 

But even before... even before all this heavy, dark stuff really took over, I was never that kind of guy. I’ve always just been a pretty even-keeled person, you know? I got my degree, I went to work, I did my job, I came home. I never had these periods where I felt on top of the world or extremely confident or anything like that. If anything, I've always been a bit on the modest side. The idea of feeling invincible or overly confident... it just sounds like a completely different person. 

And the sleep thing... needing less sleep? No, never. I mean, my sleep is a complete mess now, mostly just lying awake in the dark wishing the night would end, or hoping I just don't wake up, like I mentioned. But I never, ever wake up feeling refreshed or energized from a lack of sleep. If I missed sleep back in the day, I’d be dragging the next morning, just like anybody else. I certainly wouldn’t be buzzing around getting a million things done. 

My wife, she’s very observant. She notices everything. If I had ever started acting completely out of character, like talking a mile a minute or bouncing off the walls or acting grandiose, she would have noticed immediately. She would have sat me right down and asked what on earth was going on with me. But she’s never had to do that. She's never seen me like that because it's never happened. The only thing she’s noticed, the only thing she's worried about, is me just sort of... fading away. So, no. No periods of being high or having all this extra energy. Never anything like that. Just this constant, heavy low.

Have you ever had an episode where your mood was so low that it met the criteria for a major depressive episode — meaning you had at least five symptoms from the SIGECAPS list nearly every day for at least two weeks, including either depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure?

SIGE... SIGECAPS? I... I'm sorry, doctor, I really don't know what that means. It sounds like a medication or a brand name or something. I don't know the medical terms or the specific checklists you guys use for these things. Five symptoms, two weeks... I mean, I can't really speak to the clinical criteria of it all. 

If you're asking about right now, well, we've been talking about how I've been feeling lately, with the chair and the emptiness and just having absolutely no interest in doing anything at all. But if you're asking if this has ever happened to me *before*? Like, years ago? No. Never. 

Like I was saying just a minute ago about being a pretty even-keeled guy... I've lived fifty-one years on this earth, got my degree, worked my career, and I have never in my entire life had a period where I felt like this. Sure, I've had bad days in the past. Everyone has bad days, right? You know, you have a stressful week at work, or the car breaks down and costs a fortune, or it rains on a weekend trip you've been planning. You feel bummed out for a day or two. You get frustrated. But it always passed. I'd wake up on Monday morning, put my tie on, and be right back at it. I never had weeks and weeks of just... this absolute nothingness. Of sitting in a leather recliner all day and wishing I wouldn't wake up. 

So, I don't know if I meet your five out of whatever list you mentioned. But if you mean have I ever had a time in my past where I completely lost interest in my life and felt this incredibly low for weeks on end... no. This is the very first time I've ever been trapped in a hole like this. And honestly, it's terrifying, mostly because I don't have any frame of reference for it. I don't know how to navigate it because I've never been here before. I've always just been the guy who handles things, you know? The one who pays the mortgage, organizes the files, and keeps the trains running on time. So no, I've never had an episode like this in the past, and I certainly wouldn't have known any medical criteria to compare it to back then even if I had.

Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt down or lost interest in things, along with several other symptoms like changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, self-esteem, or thoughts of death or suicide?

Well, like I was just saying, I've never had a period like this in my past, but if you're asking about what I'm going through right now... yes, it's definitely been longer than two weeks. All those things you just listed—the sleep being a total mess, having zero energy, the thoughts about just wanting to drift off and not wake up—this has all been going on for about a month now. 

It started... well, it really all started ever since my daughter left for college out of state. We drove her up there, and it was this massive ordeal, you know? Weeks of preparing. Packing up the SUV to the brim, buying those specific extra-long twin sheets they need for the dorms, getting the mini-fridge, making sure her laptop was set up on the campus Wi-Fi. I was doing my usual thing during all of that—organizing, carrying boxes, being the dad, making sure everything was handled. I felt completely normal. 

But then... we said our goodbyes, and my wife and I drove back home. And we walked through the front door, and the house was just... silent. I mean, deafeningly quiet. That was exactly a month ago. And ever since that specific weekend, it's just been this rapid, terrifying downhill slide into this heavy emptiness. 

I thought maybe it was just normal empty nest stuff at first, you know? You read articles about that, people talk about missing their kids when they leave. I figured I'd be a little sad for a few days and then get back to normal. But this isn't just missing her. It's like the moment she left, the entire color was just drained out of my world, and for the last thirty days, I haven't been able to get it back. I walk past her bedroom door, and it's shut, and I just feel this physical weight pressing down on my chest, and I end up right back in that recliner. So, yes, it's been a solid month of this. A whole month of feeling completely hollowed out.

patient.answer:
Well, yes. Yes, I suppose that's true. I mean, it's not like I was out climbing mountains or, you know, going to fancy galas before, but I had things that mattered to me. Things I used to actually look forward to. 

Like my model railway... I don't know if I mentioned that, but I have this whole setup down in the basement. HO scale, mostly mid-century locomotives, and I was in the middle of building this incredibly detailed switching yard. I'd spend hours down there, getting the ballast just right, painting the little figures... it was meticulous work, but it was soothing, you know? It gave me a sense of accomplishment. But now? Now the trains just sit there, half-built on the table. The glue is probably dried out in the bottles. I walk down the stairs sometimes, just to look at it, and I just feel... nothing. Or worse than nothing, I feel like it's a monument to how useless I am. I can't even bring myself to pick up a paintbrush. It just seems so utterly pointless. 

And it's not just the trains, either. It's the Cubs games. My daughter and I, we used to watch the Cubs all the time. It was our thing. Even when she got older and busier with high school, she'd still come sit on the couch with me for at least a few innings. We'd talk about the roster, complain about the bullpen... it was just nice. It was a connection. But now that she's gone, I tried turning a game on the other night. I thought, you know, maybe it'll feel normal. Maybe it'll be a distraction. But I couldn't even make it through the first inning. The sound of the crowd, the announcers... it just felt hollow. It just reminded me that she wasn't there, and that I'm just this guy sitting alone in a quiet house, not contributing anything to the world. So I turned the TV off. I haven't turned it back on since. Even the thought of opening a game on the TV just feels completely pointless now. Everything just feels... flat. Like all the color has been drained out of my life, and I'm just going through the motions, but even the motions are too heavy to keep up with.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day, which would support a diagnosis of major depressive disorder (F32.2) over adjustment disorder with depressed mood (F43.22).
doctor.question: Have you been feeling fatigued or lacking energy most days, even when you haven’t done anything physically or mentally demanding?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: Even simple things like carrying laundry upstairs or sorting the mail feel like I'm moving through wet cement, no matter how long I've been in bed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling fatigued or lacking energy most days, which directly corresponds to the Fatigue symptom.

patient.answer:
Fatigue? Oh, absolutely. It’s... it's honestly overwhelming. I mean, it’s not like I’m running marathons or, you know, even going into an office anymore, so you'd think I’d be well-rested, right? I spend most of my time just sitting around the house. But it’s this deep, heavy exhaustion that just never goes away. 

It’s like... well, the other day, I needed to bring a basket of laundry upstairs. Just a regular load, nothing crazy. And I stood at the bottom of the stairs looking up at them, and it felt like I was staring at Mount Everest. I finally picked up the basket, and every step... it honestly felt like I was moving through wet cement. My arms felt heavy, my legs felt like lead. I had to stop halfway up just to catch my breath, and not because my heart was racing or anything, but just because my body simply didn't want to move anymore. 

And it’s not just physical stuff, either. Even something as simple as sorting the mail... I went out to the mailbox, which is just at the end of the driveway, mind you, and brought in a handful of envelopes. I sat down at the kitchen table to go through them—junk mail, a couple of bills, you know the drill—and I just stared at them. The sheer effort of opening an envelope, of looking at a piece of paper and figuring out what to do with it... it was just too much. I ended up leaving it all in a pile on the table and going back to the couch. 

It doesn't matter how long I've been in bed, either. I could lie there for ten hours, twelve hours, and I wake up feeling just as drained as when I went to sleep. It’s this constant, pervasive lack of energy that just drags me down all day long, no matter what I do or don't do. I just... I don't have the energy for anything anymore. Not for the trains, not for the mail, not even to walk up a flight of stairs without feeling like I've run a decathlon. It's just exhausting, doctor. Completely exhausting.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences insomnia or hypersomnia, which helps differentiate between major depressive disorder and persistent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble sleeping — either not being able to fall asleep, waking up during the night, or sleeping much more than usual?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: I lie in bed for hours with the house too quiet, then wake up around three or four in the morning and can't get back to sleep because my mind starts running through everything I've messed up.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my sleep patterns, specifically trouble falling asleep, waking up during the night, or sleeping too much, which matches my symptom of sleep disturbance.

patient.answer:
Sleep? Oh... sleep is just a joke at this point. It's honestly a whole other battle. You'd think, given how completely exhausted I am all day, like I was just saying, that I'd just pass out the second my head hits the pillow. But no. No, it doesn't work like that at all. 

The nights might actually be the worst part of all of this, if you can believe it. Because when evening comes and I finally go up to bed... the house is just so quiet. It's too quiet. When my daughter was here, there was always some background noise, you know? The faint sound of her music, or her talking on the phone, or just the floorboards creaking. But now... it’s just this heavy, dead silence. I just lie there in the dark for hours. I stare at the ceiling, I flip the pillow, I look at the clock... and I just lie there, wide awake, listening to the silence. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off—usually just from pure, physical exhaustion—it never lasts. It’s like clockwork. I’ll jolt awake, and I’ll look over at the red numbers on the alarm clock, and it's always right around three or four in the morning. The absolute dead of night. And once my eyes are open at 3 AM, that's it. I'm done. There is absolutely no chance I'm getting back to sleep. 

I try, I really do try to close my eyes and force it, but my mind just... it just turns on and starts running at a hundred miles an hour. And it's never good thoughts. It immediately starts running through everything I've ever messed up. It’s like a highlight reel of all my failures. I lie there thinking about how I have this graduate degree that I'm doing absolutely nothing with, how I haven't provided the life my family deserved, every little time I lost my temper or wasn't there enough for my daughter... just a relentless loop of every mistake, every regret. You can't sleep when your own brain is just screaming at you about what a massive disappointment you are. So I just end up lying there, trapped in my own head, until the sun finally comes up. And by then, I'm already too exhausted to face the day.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had a prior episode of major depression that would differentiate F32.2 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder) from F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood)
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced a period in your life before this recent one where you felt this level of hopelessness, guilt, or loss of interest in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my psychiatric history, specifically if I have experienced similar depressive episodes in the past, which is not covered by any of the current symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
No... no, honestly, I haven't. I mean, sure, I've had bad days, or even bad weeks. Who hasn't, right? Life gets stressful. I remember back when I was finishing up my graduate degree, the pressure was just immense. I'd have these moments where I felt completely overwhelmed, maybe a little down, wondering if I was ever going to get through my thesis and all the expectations. Or, you know, when my daughter was little and money was tight, there were nights I'd sit up worrying about how we'd pay for everything, feeling the weight of being a provider. 

But even then... even when things were really hard, it was never... it was never *this*. With those things, there was always a light at the end of the tunnel. I always knew, deep down, that if I just kept pushing, things would get better. I could still laugh at a joke, or I could still go down to the basement and tinker with the trains and actually feel some relief. I could still enjoy a baseball game and forget my troubles for a few hours. 

But this? This is entirely different. I've never experienced anything close to this level of just... absolute, crushing emptiness. It’s like a completely different species of feeling. I used to think I was a pretty resilient guy, you know? I thought I could handle whatever life threw at me, that I had a good head on my shoulders. I look back at those times I thought I was struggling before, and they honestly seem like a walk in the park compared to this. I just never knew a person's mind could turn on them so completely, where you just feel utterly hopeless and guilty for even taking up space in the world. So, no, doctor, this is all completely new to me. And it's terrifying, frankly, because I don't know how to get back to the guy who could just shake off a bad week.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any significant change in appetite or weight related to their current symptoms.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently — like eating much less or much more than usual, or losing or gaining a significant amount of weight?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: Most days I don't bother making a real meal, and I've had to tighten my belt because I forget to eat until late and then only manage toast or cereal.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite and weight, which directly corresponds to the Weight_Appetite_Change symptom.

patient.answer:
Appetite? Yeah... yeah, that's gone too. It's funny you ask that because I was just thinking about it the other day when I was trying to put on a pair of pants I haven't worn in a while. I had to pull my belt tight, like, two notches tighter than usual. I hadn't really noticed until then, but I guess I've lost quite a bit of weight. It’s not like I’m trying to, believe me. I just... I don't care about food anymore. 

It used to be that dinner was a whole thing, you know? My wife would cook, or I'd grill something out back, and we'd sit down together. It was an event. But now? Most days, I just don't even bother making a real meal. The thought of getting up, figuring out what to cook, getting the ingredients out, standing by the stove... it just goes back to that exhaustion I was talking about earlier. It's just too much effort. It feels completely pointless to go through all that trouble just for myself. 

So, what happens is, I just sit there on the couch, or I'm lying in bed, and I honestly just forget to eat. The whole day will go by, and I won't even realize I haven't had anything until it's, like, eight or nine at night and my stomach starts making these awful hollow noises. And even then, when I finally realize I should probably put something in my stomach, I don't have the energy or the desire to actually make anything substantial. I'll just shuffle into the kitchen and pop a couple of pieces of bread in the toaster. Or I'll pour a bowl of cereal. That's about all I can manage. Just dry toast or a bowl of Cheerios, standing there in the dark kitchen. And even then, I'm just forcing it down. It all tastes like cardboard anyway. There's no joy in it, no flavor, no satisfaction. It's just... fuel, I guess, but barely even that. So yeah, I'm definitely eating a lot less, and the weight is just falling off because of it.

doctor.intent: Assess the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation, which helps differentiate between severe and persistent depressive disorder
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or feeling restless and unable to sit still?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or retardation, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Restless? No... no, definitely not restless. I mean, to be restless, you have to actually have some kind of energy, right? Like a nervous energy or a need to do something. And I have absolutely zero energy. It's funny you ask about sitting still, because sitting still is pretty much the only thing I actually *do* anymore. 

I have this old leather recliner in the living room—it’s right by the front window where you can see out onto the street—and I’ll just sit there. For hours and hours. I don't fidget, I don't pace the floors, I don't tap my foot... I just sit. It’s almost like I’m glued to the chair. I'll watch the cars go by, or the mailman doing his route, and I just feel completely rooted there, like I'm just another heavy piece of furniture in the room. So no, I'm definitely not unable to sit still. If anything, I'm way too still. I just want to sink into the cushions and disappear. 

And as for moving or speaking slowly... I really don't think so? I mean, I'm not exactly sprinting around the house, obviously, because of how completely exhausted I am, but when I do finally get up to, say, go make that piece of toast I mentioned earlier, I just walk normally, I think. I don't feel like I'm moving through molasses or slow motion or anything like that. 

And my speech... well, you're listening to me right now. I feel like I'm talking at the exact same pace I always have. My wife hasn't pointed anything out about it, either. We don't talk nearly as much these days, mostly because I just don't have the drive to hold a real conversation, but when I do say something, it comes out normal. I haven't noticed my words dragging. I'm just... I'm just completely drained, you know? But not physically slow or restless. Just stuck.

inference.note: The patient continues to meet criteria for Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent, Severe (F32.2) with no evidence of symptoms suggestive of other disorders such as anxiety disorders or bipolar disorder. Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood (F43.22) remains on the list as the onset of symptoms followed a psychosocial stressor (daughter leaving for college) and a distinction between a normal bereavement-like adjustment and a major depressive episode remains important to make. Further clarification is still needed to determine if this is a major depressive episode superimposed on an adjustment reaction or if the entire clinical picture fits better under F32.2.

doctor.intent: Assess presence of suicidal ideation to evaluate severity and safety concerns.
doctor.question: Have you had any thoughts about ending your life or not wanting to live anymore?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I've been having thoughts that it would be easier if I didn't wake up, and it scared me when I caught myself going over my finances like I was getting things ready for someone else.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of ending my life or not wanting to live anymore, which directly maps to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
I... well, I wouldn't say I have a specific plan or anything like that. I'm not sitting here actively figuring out how to do it. But... wanting to live? That's a much harder question to answer lately. Because, honestly, there are so many nights now where I just lie there in the dark, and I think about how much easier it would be if I just didn't wake up the next morning. You know? If I just drifted off and that was it. No more waking up to this heavy, crushing emptiness I was telling you about. No more dragging myself out of bed just to sit in that recliner all day feeling like a burden. Just... peace. Just quiet. I've had that thought a lot, actually. Just hoping I'd go to sleep and the universe would just sort of take care of it for me, so I wouldn't have to face another single day feeling like this. 

But then... there was this thing that happened a few days ago that really, really shook me up. It actually scared me quite a bit. I was sitting at the dining room table—which I rarely do anymore, like I said, I'm usually just glued to that chair by the window—but I had my laptop open, and I had all these folders pulled out. The bank statements, the life insurance policy, the mortgage documents. And I was organizing them. I was making sure all the account numbers were clearly listed out on this yellow legal pad, writing down the passwords, checking the beneficiaries to make sure everything was completely up to date. I was just meticulously going through every single financial detail we have. 

And I was sitting there, writing it all out, and it suddenly hit me like a ton of bricks *why* I was doing it. I wasn't just doing our regular monthly budget or checking our balances. I was... I was getting things ready. I was setting it all up so that if I wasn't here, my wife wouldn't have to struggle to figure out where everything was. I was preparing it all for someone else to take over. And when I realized that—when I caught myself actually preparing for not being around—it terrified me. It really did. Because I didn't even consciously sit down with the intention to do that, my brain just sort of took me there on autopilot. So, I guess... I guess the thoughts are definitely there, even if I'm trying to ignore them. It's just getting so incredibly hard to keep carrying all this weight every day.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had a manic or hypomanic episode, which would differentiate F32.2 (Major Depressive Disorder, Severe) from F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood).
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced a period of time where you felt unusually high, overly energetic, or extremely confident — maybe even to the point where others noticed you were acting out of character or needed less sleep?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of mania or hypomania (feeling unusually high, overly energetic, extremely confident, needing less sleep), which are not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Unusually high? Energetic? No... no, I can honestly say I have never felt anything even close to that. It’s actually almost hard to even imagine feeling that way right now, to be perfectly honest with you. I mean, you’re asking about having too much energy, and like I was saying earlier about the toast and just sitting in that recliner all day, I barely have the energy to just exist right now. 

But even before... even before all this heavy, dark stuff really took over, I was never that kind of guy. I’ve always just been a pretty even-keeled person, you know? I got my degree, I went to work, I did my job, I came home. I never had these periods where I felt on top of the world or extremely confident or anything like that. If anything, I've always been a bit on the modest side. The idea of feeling invincible or overly confident... it just sounds like a completely different person. 

And the sleep thing... needing less sleep? No, never. I mean, my sleep is a complete mess now, mostly just lying awake in the dark wishing the night would end, or hoping I just don't wake up, like I mentioned. But I never, ever wake up feeling refreshed or energized from a lack of sleep. If I missed sleep back in the day, I’d be dragging the next morning, just like anybody else. I certainly wouldn’t be buzzing around getting a million things done. 

My wife, she’s very observant. She notices everything. If I had ever started acting completely out of character, like talking a mile a minute or bouncing off the walls or acting grandiose, she would have noticed immediately. She would have sat me right down and asked what on earth was going on with me. But she’s never had to do that. She's never seen me like that because it's never happened. The only thing she’s noticed, the only thing she's worried about, is me just sort of... fading away. So, no. No periods of being high or having all this extra energy. Never anything like that. Just this constant, heavy low.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode, which is required for a diagnosis of F32.2 (Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent, Severe), as the patient has not had previous episodes and the current episode is less than 2 years in duration.
doctor.question: Have you ever had an episode where your mood was so low that it met the criteria for a major depressive episode — meaning you had at least five symptoms from the SIGECAPS list nearly every day for at least two weeks, including either depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a past history of major depressive episodes, which is not covered by the current symptom profile.

patient.answer:
SIGE... SIGECAPS? I... I'm sorry, doctor, I really don't know what that means. It sounds like a medication or a brand name or something. I don't know the medical terms or the specific checklists you guys use for these things. Five symptoms, two weeks... I mean, I can't really speak to the clinical criteria of it all. 

If you're asking about right now, well, we've been talking about how I've been feeling lately, with the chair and the emptiness and just having absolutely no interest in doing anything at all. But if you're asking if this has ever happened to me *before*? Like, years ago? No. Never. 

Like I was saying just a minute ago about being a pretty even-keeled guy... I've lived fifty-one years on this earth, got my degree, worked my career, and I have never in my entire life had a period where I felt like this. Sure, I've had bad days in the past. Everyone has bad days, right? You know, you have a stressful week at work, or the car breaks down and costs a fortune, or it rains on a weekend trip you've been planning. You feel bummed out for a day or two. You get frustrated. But it always passed. I'd wake up on Monday morning, put my tie on, and be right back at it. I never had weeks and weeks of just... this absolute nothingness. Of sitting in a leather recliner all day and wishing I wouldn't wake up. 

So, I don't know if I meet your five out of whatever list you mentioned. But if you mean have I ever had a time in my past where I completely lost interest in my life and felt this incredibly low for weeks on end... no. This is the very first time I've ever been trapped in a hole like this. And honestly, it's terrifying, mostly because I don't have any frame of reference for it. I don't know how to navigate it because I've never been here before. I've always just been the guy who handles things, you know? The one who pays the mortgage, organizes the files, and keeps the trains running on time. So no, I've never had an episode like this in the past, and I certainly wouldn't have known any medical criteria to compare it to back then even if I had.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode in the past, as defined by DSM-5 criteria (i.e., five or more symptoms of depression nearly every day for at least two weeks), to differentiate between F32.2 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder) and F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood).
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt down or lost interest in things, along with several other symptoms like changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, self-esteem, or thoughts of death or suicide?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a month, ever since my daughter left for college out of state.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has experienced a depressive episode lasting at least two weeks. The patient can answer this by confirming the duration of their current episode, which has lasted for one month.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying, I've never had a period like this in my past, but if you're asking about what I'm going through right now... yes, it's definitely been longer than two weeks. All those things you just listed—the sleep being a total mess, having zero energy, the thoughts about just wanting to drift off and not wake up—this has all been going on for about a month now. 

It started... well, it really all started ever since my daughter left for college out of state. We drove her up there, and it was this massive ordeal, you know? Weeks of preparing. Packing up the SUV to the brim, buying those specific extra-long twin sheets they need for the dorms, getting the mini-fridge, making sure her laptop was set up on the campus Wi-Fi. I was doing my usual thing during all of that—organizing, carrying boxes, being the dad, making sure everything was handled. I felt completely normal. 

But then... we said our goodbyes, and my wife and I drove back home. And we walked through the front door, and the house was just... silent. I mean, deafeningly quiet. That was exactly a month ago. And ever since that specific weekend, it's just been this rapid, terrifying downhill slide into this heavy emptiness. 

I thought maybe it was just normal empty nest stuff at first, you know? You read articles about that, people talk about missing their kids when they leave. I figured I'd be a little sad for a few days and then get back to normal. But this isn't just missing her. It's like the moment she left, the entire color was just drained out of my world, and for the last thirty days, I haven't been able to get it back. I walk past her bedroom door, and it's shut, and I just feel this physical weight pressing down on my chest, and I end up right back in that recliner. So, yes, it's been a solid month of this. A whole month of feeling completely hollowed out.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's reason for seeking psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for a severe major depressive episode (F32.2) based on the presence of core symptoms including depressed mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, fatigue, and suicidal ideation, all occurring in a continuous episode of one month duration without prior episodes or manic features. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood (F43.22) was considered but ruled out due to the full major depressive syndrome and duration exceeding typical adjustment responses.
